title: Spacecraft Triumphs Over Glitch, Reaches Mercury After 8‑Year Voyage – CBS News
body:
The European‑Japanese probe BepiColombo finally slipped into orbit around Mercury on Thursday, concluding an eight‑year odyssey that began with a launch from French Guiana in October 2018. The spacecraft’s arrival marks the first time a probe has successfully entered the innermost planet’s gravitational grip after a complex, multi‑planet cruise, and it comes despite a brief but potentially mission‑ending software glitch that forced engineers to rewrite the probe’s navigation plan on the fly.

BepiColombo is actually a pair of spacecraft – the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) built by the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Mio (or Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter) supplied by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). After launch, the duo spent three years in a series of gravity‑assist flybys of Earth, Venus and Mercury itself, using each planetary encounter to shave precious velocity and reshape its trajectory. The final maneuver, a 15‑minute engine burn in late August 2025, slowed the probe enough for Mercury’s gravity to capture it into a highly elliptical orbit, setting the stage for a year‑long science campaign.

The mission’s biggest technical hurdle emerged in early July when telemetry indicated that the MPO’s attitude‑control system had entered an unexpected mode, causing the spacecraft to point its solar arrays away from the Sun for several minutes. The anomaly threatened to deplete the probe’s power reserves and could have forced a premature end to the cruise phase. ESA engineers quickly diagnosed the issue as a software timing error in the on‑board guidance algorithm, uploaded a patch from Earth, and verified that the system had returned to normal operation. The swift response not only averted a crisis but also demonstrated the robustness of the mission’s redundancy architecture, which includes separate flight computers and backup power channels.

Scientists are now eager to exploit BepiColombo’s unique payload suite, which combines ESA’s high‑resolution cameras, spectrometers and a laser altimeter with JAXA’s magnetometer and plasma instruments. The mission aims to answer long‑standing questions about Mercury’s extreme environment: why the planet’s magnetic field is unexpectedly strong for its size, how its surface has been reshaped by a relentless barrage of solar wind and micrometeoroids, and what clues its geology holds about the early solar system. Early data from the MPO’s remote‑sensing suite already hint at previously unseen hollows—shallow, bright depressions thought to result from volatile loss—suggesting that Mercury’s surface chemistry may be more dynamic than previously believed.

BepiColombo’s successful orbit insertion also carries broader implications for deep‑space exploration. The mission’s eight‑year cruise, which relied on a series of gravity assists rather than a direct, fuel‑intensive trajectory, showcases a cost‑effective model for reaching difficult destinations. Moreover, the collaborative framework between ESA and JAXA underscores the growing trend of multinational partnerships pooling expertise, technology and funding to tackle ambitious scientific goals. As space agencies worldwide contemplate missions to the Sun’s corona, the icy moons of the outer planets, and even interstellar probes, BepiColombo stands as a proof‑of‑concept that complex, long‑duration missions can be managed successfully through shared risk and coordinated problem‑solving.

Looking ahead, the spacecraft will spend the next twelve months gradually lowering its orbit, allowing its instruments to scan Mercury’s polar craters for water‑ice deposits, map the planet’s magnetic field in unprecedented detail, and monitor how solar radiation interacts with its exosphere. The data returned will feed into models that could refine predictions of space‑weather impacts on Earth’s own technological infrastructure. With its orbit now secured, BepiColombo is poised to deliver a treasure trove of discoveries that will reshape our understanding of the solar system’s innermost world and set the stage for the next generation of planetary explorers.
